Nvidia set the tone for Asian trade on Wednesday, with results and a strong outlook lifting chip stocks across the region, while gold fell below $3,800 as markets braced for another Federal Reserve rate hike.

Nvidia and equities

Nvidia beat forecasts in its first report since Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive. Third-quarter revenue rose 103% to around $116 billion, and the company guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130 billion, above estimates of about $125 billion. On the earnings call, interim chief executive Colette Kress forecast revenue growth of about 75% in fiscal 2028, pointed to a cloud-industry backlog of $2.5 trillion, and said Nvidia intends to return all excess free cash flow to shareholders.

Governance questions remain. Chairman Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang and has hired Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent chief executive. The Wall Street Journal reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, including whether its disclosures misled investors, and the company has not yet filed its quarterly 10-Q, breaking with past practice. Nvidia’s financial role in the AI industry is also under scrutiny, with total commitments of about $518 billion, according to the Financial Times. In contrast, TSMC is reportedly asking some AI chip customers to pay cash up front.

Nasdaq 100 futures gave back part of their early gains and were up around 0.7%, with S&P 500 futures up about 0.3%. In Asia, South Korea’s memory makers led. SK Hynix rose about 4% and Samsung Electronics about 1.4%, lifting the Kospi almost 2%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained around 0.7%, although the broader Topix slipped, while the Hang Seng fell about 1.1% and the Shanghai Composite eased 0.4%.

Gold

Gold fell below $3,800 to its lowest in more than a year as markets priced in a near-certain December Fed hike. Spot gold was down about 1.5% at around $3,791 after touching a low near $3,781, and silver dropped almost 3% to around $46. With US 10-year yields near 5.1% and the dollar close to a 19-month high, the metal has lost support. Goldman Sachs has cut its end-2026 gold target to $4,150 from $4,650.

Australia

Australian wages rose 1.1% in the September quarter, the fastest pace in nearly three years, lifting annual growth to 3.5%. Award wage rises drove private sector pay and frontline workers lifted the public sector, but real wages fell for a fourth straight quarter. The result adds to the Reserve Bank of Australia’s inflation worries after a split vote lifted rates to 4.85% this month, yet swaps still imply about a 75% chance that rates have peaked. AUD/USD edged down to around 0.6724 ahead of Thursday’s jobs report. In New Zealand, producer price growth slowed in the third quarter, with input prices up 0.7% and output prices up 0.8%.

Japan

Japan’s exports rose for a 14th straight month to a record ¥11.8 trillion in October, up 20.5% on AI-related chip demand. Imports also set a record but rose less than expected, narrowing the trade deficit to around ¥477 billion. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said the bank will keep raising rates in line with economic and price developments, keeping a December hike in play. Morgan Stanley reiterated its preference for long USD/JPY, which held around 159.4 near Tokyo’s intervention line. The 10-year JGB yield was little changed near 2.87%.

Oil

Oil eased with Brent down about 0.5% at around $92.65 and WTI down about 1% near $83.80. Prices remain elevated because of the Iran war, which continues to drive Japan’s energy import bill and feed inflation pressure that keeps the Fed tightening.

Ahead

The minutes of the Fed’s October meeting are due later in the US session, followed by Australian jobs data on Thursday and Japan’s national inflation figures on Friday.

item.title: What tokenized stock supply shows that price and volume miss: the Nvidia test
item.description:
Supply data is still a niche signal, but it gives traders something price charts cannot: a view of whether onchain holders are adding or withdrawing capital during a shock. For issuers and listed names tied to the sector, such as Robinhood and Coinbase, sustained supply growth through volatility supports the case that tokenized equities draw lasting demand rather than novelty trading. The metric has no direct read-through to BTC or ETH, though it does reflect risk appetite among crypto-native investors reaching into traditional assets. A supply divergence that persists after the price recovers would be a stronger signal than one that reverses through redemptions.

---

Earlier re this:

  • Onchain investors bought Nvidia’s Huang sell-off: tokenized supply up 121% in a week

And, earlier on earnings etc:

  • Nvidia (price up) tops forecasts by $7 billion as Kress steers first report since Huang exit
  • Nvidia hands three directors export control oversight days after Huang exit
  • SEC reportedly probes Nvidia disclosures as Bessent demands answers within 10 days
  • Nvidia board shuts the door on Huang’s return, refuses to discuss his exit on call
  • Nvidia sees 75% revenue growth next year as Kress points to $2.5 trillion backlog
  • Nvidia’s missing 10-Q: three reasons to be alert, not alarmed
  • Supplier, lender, shareholder: how Nvidia became the "Bank of AI"
  • Back to the future! Nvidia earnings/forecast lifts Nasdaq futures 1.3%

---

Volume tells you a token changed hands, supply tells you someone wanted more of it, and Nvidia’s week of turmoil showed how different those two stories can be.

Summary:

  • Tokenized stocks are blockchain tokens backed one-for-one by real shares held with custodians, issued by firms such as bStocks, xStocks and Robinhood.
  • New tokens are minted when an authorized participant subscribes and the issuer buys the underlying share. Redemptions take tokens out of circulation.
  • Volume measures tokens changing hands. Supply measures how many exist, so a rising supply count signals net new demand.
  • In the week Jensen Huang resigned, tokenized Nvidia supply rose 121% to about 2.3 million tokens while the shares fell 13%.
  • Limits: intermediaries often do the minting, the amounts are small, supply is spread across about 18 versions, and redemptions can reverse a surge.

When Nvidia shares fell 13% in the week Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, the supply of tokenized Nvidia stock rose 121% to about 2.3 million tokens, according to Token Terminal data shared by Token Relations. The two numbers point in opposite directions, and the reason they can do that explains one of the more useful metrics in the tokenized equity market.

A tokenized stock is a blockchain token designed to track a listed share one-for-one. Issuers such as bStocks, Kraken’s xStocks and Robinhood hold the underlying shares with custodians and issue tokens against them. New tokens are created when an authorized participant subscribes with the issuer, which buys the real share to back it. When tokens are redeemed, they are returned to the issuer and taken out of circulation.

That process makes supply a different measure from trading volume. Volume counts tokens changing hands, and every sale needs a buyer, so heavy volume can mean fear, enthusiasm or simple churn. Supply counts how many tokens exist. It only rises when someone wants enough new exposure for fresh shares to be bought and wrapped, and it only falls when holders hand tokens back. A rising supply line is a footprint of net new demand.

Read that way, the Nvidia chart tells a clear story. Supply began climbing around November 9 and 10, after the company’s board announced an independent investigation, and kept rising through the November 12 resignation while the price slid to around $156. Onchain investors were adding exposure into the decline, not leaving.

The metric has limits. New tokens are often created by market makers and other intermediaries, so a supply jump shows demand reaching the market without showing exactly who the end buyers are. The amounts are also small: 2.3 million tokens is roughly $360 million of exposure, a fraction of Nvidia’s value of several trillion dollars. Supply is split across about 18 versions on different chains, so one issuer’s figures can mislead. And redemptions can unwind a surge as quickly as it built.

Used with those caveats, supply works best as a sentiment gauge alongside price. When the two diverge, as they did for Nvidia, it suggests onchain holders see the move differently from the wider market, and the next step is watching whether that supply holds once the price recovers. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Recap: Australian wages grow at fastest pace in nearly 3 years, yet swaps see a 75% RBA peak
item.description:
The Australian dollar barely moved, holding around 0.67, because traders treated the data as backward-looking and are focused on Thursday’s jobs report. Swaps still lean towards a peak in rates. A firm jobs number would challenge that, lifting front-end yields and supporting the currency, while a rise in unemployment would reinforce bets on easing by 2027. The contrast between strong wage growth and rising layoffs creates two-way risk for Australian bank stocks and rate-sensitive retailers, especially given the job cuts at David Jones and Bunnings. Watch the jobless rate on Thursday more closely than the headline jobs figure.

--- Australia now has wages, interest rates and unemployment all rising together, which leaves the RBA choosing between the pay data and the layoff headlines.

Summary:

  • The wage price index rose 1.1% q/q in Q3, the fastest since late 2023, ahead of forecasts of 0.9% to 1.0%
  • Annual growth was 3.5%, with the private sector at 3.4% and the public sector at 3.9%
  • The 4.75% award wage increase drove private pay, and rises for state frontline workers lifted public pay
  • Real wages fell 0.4% y/y, a fourth straight quarterly decline
  • Unemployment is at a five-year high of 4.7%, and David Jones and Bunnings are cutting jobs
  • Swaps imply about a 75% chance the RBA has peaked, ahead of Thursday’s jobs data

Australian wages grew at their fastest pace in nearly three years in the September quarter, giving the Reserve Bank of Australia more reason to keep policy tight even as cracks appear in the jobs market.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said its wage price index rose 1.1% in the quarter, the strongest result since late 2023. That broke a run of five quarters at around 0.8% and topped forecasts of between 0.9% and 1.0%. Annual growth picked up to 3.5% from 3.2%. Private sector pay rose 3.4% over the year and public sector pay 3.9%, Reuters reported.

The ABS pointed to two drivers. The Fair Work Commission’s 4.75% increase in minimum and award wages from July lifted private sector pay, while raises for state government frontline workers pushed up public sector wages. Public sector pay has now outpaced the private sector for seven straight quarters. Real wages are still going backwards, down 0.4% over the year, the fourth consecutive quarter of decline.

For the RBA, the harder question is what it may take to bring inflation down. If pay keeps rising at this rate, the bank may have to tolerate a jobless rate higher than it currently projects, possibly above the level it regards as consistent with steady inflation. The central bank has argued that the labour market is easing, yet pay growth shows little sign of cooling broadly. And unless productivity picks up, wage gains of this size sit uneasily with inflation returning to the 2% to 3% band. For households, at least, bigger pay rises offer some relief after a long squeeze.

The bank lifted rates for a fifth time this year in November, to an 18-year high of 4.85%, partly because it judged the labour market to be a little tight. Three board members opposed the move, concerned the economy could be heading for a materially sharper downturn. One economist noted that Australia is in the unusual position of having unemployment, interest rates and wages all rising at once, and said wage growth and joblessness are likely to stay elevated through 2027.

There are signs that the labour market is weakening. Unemployment hit a five-year high of 4.7% in September, and layoffs are spreading. Department store David Jones plans to cut 1,500 jobs by the end of the year, and hardware chain Bunnings said this week it would cut around 230 permanent roles.

That puts Thursday’s employment report in focus. Forecasts point to a rise of 25,000 jobs in October and an unchanged unemployment rate of 4.7%.

Markets largely looked through the wage figures, treating them as backward-looking. Swaps still imply about a 75% chance that the RBA has finished raising rates, with roughly 20 basis points of easing priced by the end of 2027. A strong jobs report on Thursday would test that confidence, while a weak one would strengthen the case of the three dissenters.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold’s worst enemy right now is a 5% Treasury yield, not the headlines from the Middle East
item.description:
A break below $3,800 removes a key psychological level and leaves gold exposed to further selling if the Fed minutes sound hawkish. Gold miners and silver are likely to stay under pressure, though silver has been holding up better in recent sessions. For traders, gold is now trading as a rates instrument: US yields and Fed pricing matter more than geopolitical headlines. A spike in oil prices from the Iran war would likely add to the pressure by lifting inflation expectations and Fed hike bets. Any dovish surprise from the Fed would be the main trigger for a short-covering bounce.

--

Earlier:

  • Goldman’s second gold forecast downgrade in a month turns its bear case into the base case

--

A year ago gold was rallying on hopes of Fed cuts. Today it is under $3,800 because the Fed is hiking, and even the Iran war is working against it.

Summary:

  • Spot gold fell about 1.4% to around $3,795, its lowest in more than a year, and futures fell almost 1.8%
  • Markets price about a 96% chance of a December Fed hike, with a small chance of 50bp
  • US 10-year yields are near 5.1%, and the dollar is near a 19-month high
  • A year ago gold was rallying on expectations of two or three Fed cuts in 2026
  • Goldman Sachs has cut its end-2026 gold target to $4,150 from $4,650
  • The minutes of the Fed’s October meeting are the next catalyst

Gold fell below $3,800 an ounce in Asian trade on Wednesday, extending a slide to its lowest in more than a year as markets brace for a Federal Reserve rate hike next month. Spot gold dropped about 1.4% to around $3,795, after touching a low near $3,792, while futures fell almost 1.8%.

The driver is the same one that has dominated the past week: a Fed that is tightening rather than easing. Markets price roughly a 96% chance of a quarter-point hike in December, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, with a small chance of a half-point move. Fed Governor Christopher Waller added to those bets last week when he said a half-point hike may be needed if core inflation runs hot. US 10-year Treasury yields are hovering around 5.1%, and the dollar is near its strongest level in 19 months.

That combination works against gold on two fronts. Higher yields raise the opportunity cost of holding a metal that pays no income, and a stronger dollar makes it more expensive for buyers using other currencies.

The contrast with a year ago is stark. In November 2025, gold was beginning its climb to a record high as markets expected two or three Fed rate cuts in 2026. Twelve months on, the outlook has flipped from easing to tightening, and gold has given back a large part of those gains.

The Iran war has not provided the support many would expect. Rather than acting as a safe haven, gold has fallen as geopolitical risk has pushed up oil prices, which feeds into inflation, firms up Fed hike expectations and lifts yields. In this cycle, escalation in the Middle East has tended to hurt gold rather than help it.

Banks are adjusting their forecasts. Goldman Sachs analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven have cut their end-2026 target to $4,150 an ounce from $4,650, arguing that a hawkish Fed could block the support gold usually gets from falling yields. Even the lower target implies a recovery of roughly 9% from current levels in a little over six weeks, which shows how quickly the outlook has shifted.

Attention now turns to the minutes of the Fed’s October meeting, due later on Wednesday in the US. A hawkish tone would reinforce December hike expectations and could push gold lower still, with some analysts watching support near $3,708. A softer message, or any sign that the Fed is uneasy about the recent sell-off in technology stocks, could give gold room to recover. For now, the market’s message is clear: as long as the Fed is hiking, gold is struggling to find buyers. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: TSMC reportedly demands cash up front from AI chip clients amid circular financing fears
item.description:
If confirmed, the move would be a vote of caution about AI customer finances from the company with the clearest view of chip demand. That would add weight to the circular financing debate that has hung over AI stocks this month. Custom chip designers and smaller AI players with stretched balance sheets would face tighter cash flow and could lose capacity to better-funded rivals. For TSMC, the policy would strengthen its pricing power and reduce its credit risk, a positive for the stock and for Taiwan’s tech-heavy market. Watch for any confirmation or denial from TSMC, which would set how seriously the report is taken.

---

While Nvidia extends credit to the AI boom, TSMC is reportedly asking its customers to show the money first, and that difference says a lot about who carries the risk.

Summary:

  • TSMC is reportedly setting credit limits for customers based on their balance sheets, payment history and default risk
  • Orders above the limit must reportedly be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure capacity
  • The policy mainly affects custom AI chip makers, several of which are raising money through bonds, equity and loans
  • The report links the change to concerns about circular financing in AI
  • TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet could not confirm it independently

TSMC has begun weighing customers’ finances before handing out chipmaking capacity, setting credit limits and asking some buyers to pay cash up front, Chinese technology outlet Kuai Keji reported, citing industry sources. TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet said it could not independently confirm it. 

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, is the world’s largest contract chipmaker. It does not design its own chips. Instead, it manufactures them for companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD and the growing number of firms building custom AI processors. Founded in Hsinchu in 1987, it produces the vast majority of the world’s most advanced chips. That gives it near-monopoly control of the capacity every AI company needs, and that leverage is what lets it set terms on who gets served first.

According to the report, TSMC now sets a credit limit for each customer based on its balance sheet. The assessment reportedly covers any history of late or unpaid bills, the customer’s standing in the industry, its business outlook and the estimated loss if it defaulted. Orders above that limit must be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure their allocated capacity. The change is said to apply mainly to makers of custom AI chips, several of which are raising money through overseas convertible bonds, equity sales and syndicated bank loans.

The report links the shift directly to concerns about circular financing in the AI industry, where companies invest in one another and then buy from each other. In effect, TSMC would be moving from allocating capacity on a first-come, first-served basis to asking customers to prove they can pay.

That fits with comments from chief executive C.C. Wei, who has said on an earnings call that capacity planning takes into account cloud providers’ capital spending, their financial condition, and the availability of power and components. TSMC has also sent staff to the United States to check on data centre construction. The company already holds large customer prepayments, around NT$234 billion at the end of June, although Kuai Keji noted these are standard accounting prepayments rather than the new credit system.

The contrast with Nvidia is striking. Nvidia is increasingly acting as a financier of the AI build-out, with commitments of about $518 billion and customer receivables of about $81 billion, according to its latest results and a Financial Times report. TSMC, sitting further up the supply chain with near-monopoly control of advanced chipmaking, appears to be heading the other way, shifting risk back onto its customers.

If confirmed, the policy would tighten cash flow for chip designers that already tie up large sums in design and packaging costs, and it would favour well-funded customers over smaller players. It would also be a sign that the company best placed to judge AI demand wants protection in case some of its customers cannot pay. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgan Stanley sees USD/JPY fair value above 170, forecasts yen at 162 by late 2027
item.description:
A tier-one bank backing USD/JPY upside at these levels puts it in direct opposition to Japan’s Ministry of Finance, which has been warning about intervention near 160. That makes the pair asymmetric: it could grind higher on rate differentials, but intervention could drop it sharply in a single session. The Fed’s repricing is the main driver, so US data and Fed speakers matter more for USD/JPY than anything from Tokyo short of intervention. The short EUR vs AUD call gets support from today’s Australian wage beat, while the CHF leg leans on the franc’s safe-haven appeal while Middle East risks persist.

-

Morgan Stanley says a well-flagged December BOJ hike is no match for a Fed that is still tightening, and it is willing to bet against the yen right at Tokyo’s line in the sand.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley says long USD/JPY is its preferred trade on its fair value model, which it has put above 170
  • It sees room for further USD/JPY gains as markets reprice expectations for Fed rate hikes
  • Its strategists forecast the yen at 162 per dollar by Q4 2027, while Goldman Sachs takes the opposite view
  • The bank is staying short EUR against AUD and CHF
  • USD/JPY is trading near 160, where Tokyo has warned about intervention

Morgan Stanley says long USD/JPY remains its preferred trade based on its fair value model, and sees room for further gains as markets reprice the outlook for Federal Reserve rate hikes. The bank has estimated fair value for the pair above 170, well above the current level of around 159.5.

Its case rests on the yen’s sensitivity to global bond yields. Morgan Stanley has described the yen as the G10 currency most exposed to rising yields worldwide, and argues there is limited room for the Bank of Japan to surprise markets with a more hawkish move than is already expected. With US yields climbing on expectations that the Fed will keep tightening, that combination continues to favour the dollar against the yen.

The longer-term view points the same way. Morgan Stanley strategists including Serena Tang forecast the yen weakening to 162 per dollar by the fourth quarter of 2027. They argue that strong global risk appetite, Japan’s terms of trade and the continued appeal of carry trades will outweigh support from narrowing interest rate differentials. Goldman Sachs has taken the opposite view on the yen, a split that shows how hard the currency has become to call.

The bank is also staying short the euro against the Australian dollar and the Swiss franc. The Australian leg looks better supported after stronger than expected wage data on Wednesday added to the case for a hawkish Reserve Bank of Australia.

The main risk to the USD/JPY trade is Tokyo. The pair is trading just below 160, where Japanese officials have stepped up warnings about intervention, and MUFG expects action somewhere between here and 164, this year’s high. The last official intervention drove the pair from around 164 to 155 in under a week, a reminder of how quickly a crowded position can unwind.

The Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise its policy rate from 1.25% in December, and Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the bank will keep tightening. Morgan Stanley’s argument is that a well-flagged hike will not be enough to turn the yen while the Fed is also raising rates. For yen bulls, the turning point would need either a pause from the Fed or a much faster pace of tightening from Tokyo. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Recap: Japan exports hit record ¥11.8 trillion as AI chip demand extends run to 14 months
item.description:
Record exports support the view that Japan’s economy can absorb a December rate hike despite the third-quarter contraction, which should keep upward pressure on short-end JGB yields. Chipmakers and chip equipment suppliers in Tokyo are the clearest beneficiaries, though the reliance on AI demand leaves them exposed to any pullback in global tech spending. Oil is the swing factor for the trade balance: crude prices tied to the Iran war set the size of Japan’s import bill, and a renewed spike would quickly widen the deficit. The yen is likely to take its direction from US-Japan rate gaps rather than the trade figures.

--- Japan is selling more than ever to an AI-hungry world, but record oil-driven import costs mean households are not sharing in the boom.

Summary:

  • Exports rose 20.5% y/y in October to a record ¥11.8 trillion, a 14th straight monthly gain, against 20% forecast
  • Exports to the US rose about 24% and to China about 13%, with chip-related goods leading
  • Imports rose 21.6% to a record ¥12.2 trillion, below the 25.8% forecast, driven by energy costs while volumes slipped
  • The trade deficit was around ¥477 billion, roughly half the forecast shortfall
  • The economy contracted in Q3 on weak consumer spending
  • BOJ Governor Ueda said the bank will keep raising rates, and markets expect a December hike

Japan’s exports rose for a 14th straight month in October and hit a record value, as global investment in artificial intelligence kept demand for chip-related shipments strong, Ministry of Finance data showed on Wednesday.

Exports climbed 20.5% from a year earlier to about ¥11.8 trillion, roughly $74 billion and the highest for any single month on record, Reuters reported. That beat the 20% median forecast and picked up from September’s 16.5% gain. Shipments to the United States rose about 24%, while exports to China increased about 13%. Analysts cited by Reuters said AI-related demand continued to support exports of semiconductors and chipmaking equipment, helping offset sluggish Chinese demand. Economists also noted that companies passing on higher costs had lifted the nominal value of shipments, so part of the gain reflects prices rather than volumes.

Imports also set a monthly record at about ¥12.2 trillion, up 21.6% from a year earlier, although that was below the 25.8% forecast. Elevated crude prices and higher transport costs pushed up the value of energy imports amid instability in the Middle East, even as import volumes slipped 0.2%. Oil remains Japan’s main exposure to the Iran war, since the country imports close to 90% of its energy.

The softer than expected import bill left a trade deficit of around ¥477 billion, about half the shortfall economists had forecast.

The data shows external demand is still supporting an economy that contracted unexpectedly in the third quarter, as higher living costs forced households to cut spending. Rising import costs are likely to keep squeezing household purchasing power and corporate margins, which means the export boom is not translating into broad domestic strength.

For the Bank of Japan, the figures add to the case for raising rates in December. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the bank will keep raising its policy rate in line with economic, price and financial developments, and that financial conditions remain accommodative. The policy rate is 1.25%. Resilient exports help offset the weak GDP reading, while import-driven inflation keeps pressure on the bank to act.

The yen has drawn little support so far. USD/JPY remains near 160, where Tokyo has warned about intervention, as the rate gap with a Federal Reserve on a hiking path dominates. The risks to the export run are a slowdown in AI investment and further escalation in the Middle East, which would lift the oil import bill again. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

While Wall Street sold Nvidia’s leadership crisis, onchain buyers minted more than a million new tokenized shares, and Kress’s first earnings beat gave them an early reason to feel good about it.

Summary:

  • Tokenized Nvidia supply rose 121% in a week to about 2.3 million tokens, according to Token Terminal data shared by Token Relations.
  • Over the same period, Nvidia shares fell 13% to around $156, after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12.
  • New tokens are issued only when buyers subscribe through the issuer, so rising supply points to net dip buying, not just turnover.
  • Supply started climbing around November 9 and 10, after the board’s November 8 investigation and before Huang’s resignation.
  • Most of the growth came through bStocks’ NVDAb, with xStocks’ NVDAx, Robinhood’s version and 15 smaller tokens making up the rest.
  • Interim CEO Colette Kress’s first report beat forecasts by about $7 billion and pointed to a $2.5 trillion backlog, and the shares rose after hours.

Holders of tokenized Nvidia stock added to their positions as the chipmaker’s shares fell through the week of Jensen Huang’s resignation, with onchain supply rising 121% to about 2.3 million tokens, according to Token Terminal data shared by Token Relations. Over the same seven days, Nvidia’s share price dropped 13% to around $156.

The supply figure says more than trading volume would. Tokenized equities are backed one-for-one by shares held with custodians, and new tokens enter circulation only when buyers subscribe for them through the issuer. A rising supply count therefore reflects net new demand rather than existing tokens changing hands, which suggests onchain investors were buying the decline rather than heading for the exit. At the week’s closing price, the 2.3 million tokens represent roughly $360 million of exposure.

The timing also stands out. The data show supply starting to climb around November 9 and 10, after Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation on November 8 and before the November 12 announcement that Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive and director. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and Harvey C. Jones became the company’s first board chair. Most of the new supply came through bStocks’ NVDAb token, with xStocks’ NVDAx, Robinhood’s version and 15 smaller tokens making up the rest.

Those buyers got an early test of their conviction overnight. As we reported, Kress’s first quarterly report since Huang’s departure topped forecasts by about $7 billion, and she pointed to a $2.5 trillion backlog while guiding for revenue growth of around 75% next year. Nvidia shares rose in after-hours trading.

The episode offers a rare look at how onchain equity holders behave during a single-stock shock. The sums are small beside Nvidia’s market value of several trillion dollars, but the direction is clear: demand for tokenized exposure rose as the price fell. The next few sessions will show whether that was conviction or a short-term trade. If supply holds or keeps growing after the post-earnings bounce, issuers will have evidence that volatility brings in buyers. If holders redeem into strength, the surge will look more like a quick dip trade than a lasting shift.

Ueda gave the market more of the same, more hikes ahead and no panic over the food tax cut, and that is exactly what a central bank heading towards December wants to say.

Summary:

  • Ueda said the BOJ will keep raising its policy rate in line with economic, price and financial developments
  • He said it is important to see inflation anchored around 2%
  • He said financial conditions remain accommodative
  • He said the impact of the government’s food consumption tax cut is likely to be limited but highly uncertain for now
  • The BOJ will assess the tax cut’s effect on underlying inflation and set policy accordingly

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the central bank will keep raising its policy rate in line with economic, price and financial developments, reaffirming the tightening path ahead of next month’s policy meeting.

Ueda said it was important to see inflation anchored around the bank’s 2% target, and noted that financial conditions remain accommodative. That suggests he sees room to lift rates further without choking off growth. His comments follow the bank’s October decision to hold its policy rate at 1.25%, when he declared that underlying inflation had reached 2% and signalled strong prospects for a hike in December.

A large part of his remarks addressed the government’s planned cut to the consumption tax on food. Ueda said the impact of the tax cut was likely to stay limited, but described its effect on the economy and on underlying inflation as highly uncertain for now. He said the bank would assess how the cut feeds through to underlying inflation and set policy accordingly.

The distinction matters for markets. A cut to the food consumption tax would mechanically lower headline inflation when it takes effect, which could make price data look softer than the underlying trend. Ueda’s focus on underlying inflation signals that the Bank of Japan is unlikely to treat a tax-driven drop in prices as a reason to stop raising rates. At the same time, his caution about the uncertainty leaves him room to adjust if the cut boosts spending more than expected.

The comments come after stronger than expected export data earlier on Wednesday, which showed shipments up 20.5% in October and a narrower than forecast trade deficit. Third-quarter GDP contracted slightly, but the bank has pointed to firm wage growth as the stronger signal.

For the yen, Ueda’s remarks reinforce expectations of a December hike without adding a new hawkish signal. With the Federal Reserve also on a hiking path, the rate gap is likely to keep USD/JPY close to the 160 level until the Bank of Japan moves faster or the Fed pauses. item.description:
The headline beat should support the Australian dollar and short-dated yields at the margin, as traders reassess how firmly they had ruled out another RBA hike. The detail limits the hawkish case, though. Private sector strength came from a one-off award decision, public sector pay is doing much of the work, and real wages are still falling, so it’s hard to argue wages are driving inflation. That mix makes a large repricing of December less likely. For AUD/USD, rate expectations at home are still competing with a Fed on a hiking path.

Australian pay growth was the strongest in nearly three years, but it still didn’t keep up with prices, which gives both camps on the RBA board something to work with.

Summary:

  • The Wage Price Index rose 1.1% q/q in Q3, the strongest quarter since late 2023, against 1.0% expected
  • Annual wage growth picked up to 3.5% from 3.2%
  • The 4.75% award wage increase drove private sector pay
  • Public sector wages rose 1.3% q/q, led by frontline workers, outpacing the private sector for a seventh straight quarter
  • Real wages fell 0.4% over the year, the fourth consecutive quarter of negative annual growth
  • The RBA’s majority judged rates not clearly sufficient at its November meeting

Australian wages rose 1.1% in the September quarter, the strongest quarterly gain since late 2023 and ahead of the 1.0% economists had expected, Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed on Wednesday. Annual growth picked up to 3.5% from 3.2%.

The Fair Work Commission’s larger than expected 4.75% increase in award wages, which mostly flows through in the September quarter, drove the lift in private sector pay. The public sector was stronger again. Public wages rose 1.3% in the quarter, driven by frontline workers, and have now outpaced private sector wages for seven consecutive quarters.

Workers are still falling behind. Real wages fell in the quarter and were down 0.4% over the year, the fourth straight quarter of negative annual growth, as inflation continued to run ahead of pay.

The data gives the Reserve Bank of Australia’s hawks more to work with. The bank lifted the cash rate to 4.85% earlier this month, its fifth hike this year and an 18-year high, on a split 6-3 vote. Minutes released on Tuesday showed the majority judged that rates were not clearly sufficient to bring inflation under control, and Governor Michele Bullock said the same day that inflation risks remain skewed to the upside. A wage print that beats forecasts feeds into services inflation, the part of the price basket the RBA has found hardest to bring down.

The doves have their own arguments in the detail. The private sector lift came from a one-off award decision rather than a tight labour market, and much of the strength sits in public sector pay set outside market pressures. Falling real wages also suggest pay is catching up with inflation rather than driving it, with unemployment at 4.7% and job advertisements declining.

Markets had all but priced out a December hike before the release. This result makes that call look less certain, but it probably does not overturn it. The monthly inflation data due before the December meeting will carry more weight. If prices also run hot, the RBA debate could shift from whether rates have peaked to whether one more hike is needed.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6654 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan’s trade deficit comes in at half the expected size as exports jump 20.5%
item.description:
The narrower deficit is mildly supportive for the yen because it reduces the yen sold to pay for imports. Rate differentials still dominate, though, and USD/JPY remains pinned near 160 while the Fed is on a hiking path. Oil is the key swing factor: Japan’s import bill is highly sensitive to crude prices during the Iran war, so any renewed rise in oil would quickly reverse today’s improvement. For the BOJ, the data adds to evidence that the economy can absorb a December hike, which could nudge short-end JGB yields higher. Exporters with heavy chip exposure should find support in Tokyo trade.

---

Chips lifted Japan’s exports and a lighter import bill halved the expected trade gap, but the yen is still taking its cue from Washington, not Tokyo.

Summary:

  • Exports rose 20.5% y/y in October, against forecasts of about 20% and September’s revised 16.5%
  • Imports rose 21.6%, against forecasts of about 26% and a revised 18.5%
  • The trade deficit was around ¥477 billion, against an expected deficit of about ¥1 trillion
  • The seasonally adjusted deficit was around ¥767 billion, against forecasts of about ¥908 billion
  • The BOJ is widely expected to raise rates from 1.25% in December
  • USD/JPY is trading around 159.5, close to 160, where Tokyo has warned about intervention

Japan’s exports rose 20.5% in October from a year earlier, slightly ahead of expectations and a clear pick-up from September’s revised 16.5%, Ministry of Finance data showed on Wednesday. Chip shipments led the gain, ending a two-month slowdown in export growth.

Imports rose 21.6%, well short of forecasts of about 26%, after an 18.5% rise in September. As a result, the trade deficit came in at around ¥477 billion. That was roughly half the ¥1 trillion or so analysts had expected and narrower than September’s revised ¥557 billion. On a seasonally adjusted basis, the deficit was around ¥767 billion, smaller than forecast but wider than the previous month.

The import figure is the surprise. The government had said crude procurement would recover in October to around year-earlier levels as tankers routed through the Suez Canal arrived, so a bigger jump in the import bill was widely expected. Energy is Japan’s main vulnerability in the Iran war. The country imports close to 90% of its energy, and high oil prices have kept its import bill elevated.

The data adds a modest tailwind to the Bank of Japan’s case for raising rates in December. The central bank held its policy rate at 1.25% in October, but Governor Kazuo Ueda signalled strong prospects for a hike at the next meeting after declaring that underlying inflation had reached the 2% target. Board member Hajime Takata said this week that rates should rise nimbly. Solid exports help offset a slight contraction in third-quarter GDP, and a narrower trade deficit means fewer yen are being sold to pay for imports.

That may not be enough to lift the yen on its own. USD/JPY is trading around 159.5, just below the 160 level where Tokyo has stepped up warnings about intervention. With the Federal Reserve on a hiking path and US 10-year yields above 5%, the rate gap still works against the yen even if the Bank of Japan hikes. The 10-year JGB yield is near 2.9%, close to its highest since late October.

The next test is Friday’s national inflation data. A firm reading alongside today’s trade figures would strengthen expectations for a December move. A rise in oil prices, on the other hand, would quickly push the import bill and the deficit back up.

The commitments show how closely Nvidia’s fortunes are now tied to the financial health of AI labs and cloud providers, not just their appetite for chips. If funding conditions for those customers tighten, Nvidia faces exposure through unpaid bills and falling stake values as well as lost orders. Memory makers are the clearest beneficiaries of the $100 billion-plus jump in supply commitments, which gives them visibility on future demand. Expect analysts to track receivables and equity gains as closely as revenue from here.

---

  • Nvidia hands three directors export control oversight days after Huang exit
  • SEC reportedly probes Nvidia disclosures as Bessent demands answers within 10 days

Nvidia no longer just sells the AI boom its chips: it underwrites suppliers, invests in customers and waits longer to be paid, which makes its balance sheet as important as its revenue line.

Summary:

  • Nvidia’s total commitments, including supply, equity investments, cloud services and leases, reached about $518 billion
  • Supply chain commitments rose more than $100 billion in three months to $390 billion, mainly for memory chips
  • Equity holdings have roughly tripled since January, and Nvidia has spent about $58 billion on stakes this fiscal year
  • Receivables rose almost a third from the previous quarter to about $81 billion, faster than revenue
  • Free cash flow of about $44 billion in the quarter gives Nvidia ample room to fund this

Nvidia’s quarterly results are usually read as a scorecard for AI chip demand. This time the balance sheet tells a second story: Nvidia is increasingly acting as a lender, investor and guaranteed buyer for the AI industry, not just its main supplier.

Half a trillion dollars in commitments Nvidia said on Tuesday it had made more than half a trillion dollars in financial commitments, the Financial Times reported. That includes $390 billion in supply chain commitments, up more than $100 billion in three months, mainly to secure memory chips. Add equity investments, cloud services and data centre leases, and the total reaches about $518 billion.

Locking in supply on that scale works much like a bank extending credit. Nvidia is guaranteeing future orders to its suppliers, which helps them fund new capacity.

Investing in its own customers The balance sheet shows how fast Nvidia’s investment book has grown. Holdings of non-marketable securities, largely stakes in private companies, rose to about $66 billion from around $22 billion in January. Listed equity holdings climbed to about $44 billion from roughly $13 billion. Nvidia spent about $58 billion buying equity stakes in the first nine months of the fiscal year. Many of those investments are in AI labs and cloud providers that also buy Nvidia chips.

Customers owe more Accounts receivable, the money customers owe for products already delivered, reached about $81 billion, up almost a third from three months earlier, according to the FT. That is faster than revenue growth of 20% over the same period.

Why be alert, but not alarmed Critics call this circular financing: Nvidia funds customers who then buy its chips, which flatters demand. The risk is real if those customers struggle to pay or to raise money. But Nvidia generated about $44 billion of free cash flow in the quarter and has said it will return all excess cash to shareholders. For now it is financing the AI build-out from strength, not stretching to keep it going. The question to watch is whether receivables and investments keep outpacing sales.

Kress used her first call as interim chief to argue that Nvidia’s growth story is accelerating, and she backed it with higher chip prices and a promise to hand back every spare dollar of cash.

Summary:

  • Kress expects revenue to grow about 75% in fiscal 2028, with enterprise revenue more than doubling
  • The cloud-industry backlog has reached $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion three months ago
  • Hopper contracts are renewing at up to twice the original price, and B300 prices are up more than 60% since launch
  • Purchase commitments rose to $390 billion in Q3. Nvidia signed new supply deals, and its roadmap is unchanged, with Vera Rubin Ultra due next year and Feynman in 2028
  • Nvidia returned a record $28 billion in Q3 and plans to return all excess free cash flow to shareholders
  • Heidrick & Struggles will lead the CEO search, and the board ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang

Nvidia expects revenue to grow about 75% in fiscal 2028, interim chief executive Colette Kress told analysts on the company’s earnings call. It was her first outlook since taking over from Jensen Huang, and it was emphatic. She also expects enterprise revenue to more than double over the year.

Kress pointed to a cloud-industry backlog of $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion three months earlier, as evidence that demand is still building. Pricing backs that up. She said Hopper GPU contracts, an older generation, have been renewed under multi-year agreements at prices up to double their original level. Prices for the newer B300 have risen more than 60% since launch, and GPU rental rates have climbed across all generations. Older hardware gaining value is unusual in the chip industry, and it suggests compute is still in short supply.

Usage is rising as well. Kress said token prices, the cost of running AI models, have fallen nearly 60% since May, which has accelerated usage and demand for compute. Agentic workloads now make up about 80% of all tokens. She expects major frontier labs to account for about 15% of data centre revenue this year.

Nvidia is spending heavily to meet that demand. Purchase commitments rose to $390 billion in the third quarter, and commitments tied to neocloud agreements reached $32 billion. Kress announced new substrate agreements with Kinsus Technology and Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and an advanced-packaging deal with Siliconware Precision Industries. She also said Nvidia would stay cautious and disciplined in its capital commitments. The product roadmap is unchanged, with Vera Rubin Ultra still expected to launch next year and the Feynman architecture to follow in 2028.

Kress also signalled a more generous approach to shareholder returns. Nvidia returned a record $28 billion in the third quarter, about $22 billion through buybacks and $6 billion in dividends, and has handed back around 65% of free cash flow so far this year. From here, she said, the company intends to return all excess free cash flow to shareholders.

Leadership was addressed briefly. Chairman Harvey Jones said the board has no plans to reinstate Huang and has hired Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search for a permanent chief executive. He declined to discuss Huang’s resignation or the board’s ongoing investigation. Kress said Nvidia’s commitments to customers and partners would not change.

The shares swung during the call, recovering early after-hours losses to trade nearly 3% higher. The 75% forecast sets a high bar for a company still without a permanent leader, but on this call, demand rather than governance drove the share price.

Nvidia also said it would not take questions about the circumstances of Huang’s resignation. That left analysts unable to explore the issue that has dominated the company for the past week, on a call that would normally focus on record AI chip demand.

Nvidia shares swung sharply in after-hours trading, falling at first before recovering to trade nearly 3% higher during the call. Investors were weighing results that comfortably beat forecasts, with third-quarter revenue of around $116 billion and fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion.

The board’s position contrasts with comments from Huang himself. Earlier on Tuesday, he said in a statement, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, that he would be honoured to return as chief executive. Sources had already told CNBC on Monday that the board was not considering reinstating him. The call made that position official.

Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director on 12 November. His departure followed the opening of a board investigation into his disclosure of a relationship with a business executive accused of being a Chinese spy. The independent board committee leading that investigation is still at work, and finance chief Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive. Jones said the company has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search for a permanent chief executive.

Pressure is also building from outside the company. The Wall Street Journal has reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, including whether its disclosures misled investors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said he wants answers from the board within 10 days. Earlier on Tuesday, Nvidia’s board also created a committee to oversee national security and export control compliance.

The board has now settled one question but left several others open. Investors have no timeline for a permanent chief executive, no findings from the investigation, and no detail on what regulators are examining. Until those answers come, the strength of Nvidia’s business may not be enough on its own to steady the stock.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SEC reportedly probes Nvidia disclosures as Bessent demands answers within 10 days
item.description:
The probe adds a fresh regulatory overhang just as the earnings beat gives the shares some relief, and it may limit how much of that rally holds. A disclosure investigation goes to the heart of how far investors can trust Nvidia’s reported numbers, particularly in Asia, where its sales have been strongest outside the US. Any evidence that chips were diverted to China would raise the risk of tighter export controls across Southeast Asia, a threat to Nvidia’s guidance and to the regional data centre build-out that supports Asian chip and server suppliers. Expect analysts to press interim CEO Colette Kress on the probe during the conference call.

---

Nvidia’s crisis has moved from the boardroom to the regulators, and the question now is whether its Asia sales figures told investors the whole story.

Summary:

  • The SEC has opened a civil investigation into Nvidia, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported, citing people familiar with the matter
  • The probe includes whether the company’s disclosures misled investors
  • Jensen Huang resigned as CEO after revelations of two extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy and one with an employee
  • Nvidia had earlier denied any unusual relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which was suspected of diverting chips to China
  • Nvidia stopped disclosing its Singapore sales last year
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has asked for answers from the board and outside counsel within 10 days

The US Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia following the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The newspaper said the civil probe includes whether the chipmaker’s disclosures misled investors, although its full scope could not be determined.

Huang stepped down after revelations of two extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with an employee, according to the Journal. Nvidia shares have fallen more than 10% since he was ousted.

The case has drawn attention to Alice Huang, then an executive at the Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials believe is working for China’s intelligence services. China has denied the allegation. Earlier this year, Nvidia denied that Jensen Huang had any unusual or unexpected relationship with her. Megaspeed was one of several companies using Nvidia chips to build AI data centres in Southeast Asia, and was suspected of diverting some of those products to China. The Commerce Department had been investigating it since late 2024, and the Journal has reported that the Justice Department is now leading several investigations involving Alice Huang.

Disclosure is a sensitive point. The Journal noted that Nvidia changed how it reports international chip sales last year, dropping a breakdown that showed its sales to Singapore, where Megaspeed was based.

Pressure from Washington is building. Congress has called for investigations, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week questioned whether Nvidia knowingly sold powerful chips to China to boost its earnings. He said he wanted answers from the board and its outside counsel within 10 days. In a statement on Tuesday, Huang said he had fallen short of the standards expected at Nvidia and took full responsibility for his mistakes.

The report landed hours before Nvidia posted quarterly results well ahead of forecasts. On the same day, the company also set up a board committee to oversee national security and export control compliance. Strong numbers may steady the stock for now, but investors are likely to weigh any revenue upside against the risk that regulators find problems in how Nvidia has accounted for and disclosed its sales in Asia. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Nvidia is putting national security oversight in the boardroom, a message aimed squarely at Washington as it tries to move past its founder’s sudden exit.

Summary:

  • Nvidia’s board has created the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee as a new standing committee
  • Director Suzanne Nora Johnson chairs it, with directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members
  • The committee will meet at least quarterly and retain independent experts in law, national security and trade compliance
  • Nvidia’s National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the committee, and to interim CEO Colette Kress on day-to-day operations
  • Chairman Harvey Jones said advanced chips and AI pose unprecedented national security challenges
  • The move comes days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO; the release does not mention him

Nvidia’s board has set up a standing committee to oversee the chipmaker’s national security policies and export control compliance. The step comes less than a week after founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive.

Director Suzanne Nora Johnson will chair the new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, with directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. Nvidia said in a statement that the committee will meet at least quarterly, both with management and in executive session. It will also retain independent outside experts in law, national security and trade compliance.

Nvidia’s existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will now report directly to the committee, as well as to interim chief executive Colette Kress for day-to-day operations. The committee will also oversee efforts to strengthen both teams.

Board chairman Harvey Jones said advanced chips and the rise of artificial intelligence and superintelligence present national security challenges without precedent. He said that as the world’s leading advanced computing company, Nvidia has a responsibility to help lead the industry’s response. He added that the company wants to work with government and industry on a framework that protects national security while still allowing innovation. Nvidia said the move reflects the board’s commitment to closer engagement with government stakeholders and to high standards of governance.

The statement does not mention Huang. He stepped down on 12 November after the board opened an investigation into his disclosure of a relationship with a business executive accused of being a Chinese spy, which China denies. That investigation, led by an independent board committee, is ongoing, and US lawmakers have demanded answers.

The announcement came on the same day Nvidia reported quarterly results well ahead of forecasts. The company guided to around $130 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, again assuming no data centre compute sales to China.

For investors, the committee matters less for the numbers than for the company’s standing in Washington. Nvidia’s business depends heavily on export licences and political goodwill, and the board appears keen to show that oversight of sensitive trade now sits at the top of the company. Whether that settles concerns will depend on what the investigation finds and on who becomes the permanent chief executive. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia (price up) tops forecasts by $7 billion as Kress steers first report since Huang exit
item.description:
A clean beat on revenue, earnings and guidance should give the bruised AI trade a lift into the Asian session. Nasdaq futures and Asia’s chip supply chain, including TSMC, SK Hynix, Samsung and Advantest, are the obvious beneficiaries. Nvidia shares rose in early after-hours trade, but the move so far is modest next to the roughly 8% swing options had priced. That suggests traders are holding back until the conference call. Lower gross margin guidance and open questions about leadership and the board investigation could cap any rally if Kress gives an unconvincing account of either.

---

Nvidia’s numbers answered the demand question emphatically, which leaves the boardroom as the only real doubt hanging over the stock.

Summary:

  • Fiscal Q3 revenue rose 103% from a year earlier to around $116 billion, against expectations of about $109 billion
  • Adjusted EPS was $2.68, against forecasts of about $2.48
  • Data centre revenue more than doubled to around $108 billion, against a consensus of about $102 billion
  • Q4 revenue is guided to $130 billion plus or minus 3%, against estimates of about $125 billion. The quarter includes an extra week, and no China data centre compute sales are assumed
  • Q4 gross margins are guided to 71% to 72%, down from around 75% in Q3
  • This is the first report under interim CEO Colette Kress, who replaced Jensen Huang after his resignation on 12 November

Nvidia beat Wall Street forecasts on revenue, earnings and guidance in its first quarterly report since founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive. The results offer investors some reassurance after a bruising month for the stock.

Revenue for the fiscal third quarter, which ended 25 October, rose 103% from a year earlier to around $116 billion. That was comfortably ahead of the roughly $109 billion analysts had expected. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.68 a share, against forecasts of about $2.48. Data centre revenue, which makes up almost all of Nvidia’s sales, more than doubled to around $108 billion, well above a consensus of about $102 billion.

The outlook was stronger still. Nvidia said in its earnings release that it expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, against estimates of about $125 billion. The quarter includes an extra week, which flatters the comparison somewhat, and the company again assumed no data centre compute sales to China. Gross margins are guided to 71% to 72%, down from around 75% in the third quarter. That is a step lower that analysts are likely to press management on.

Colette Kress, interim chief executive and still the finance chief, said the company’s momentum was real. She described the start of the new Vera Rubin platform as explosive. Nvidia said Vera Rubin NVL72 systems have shipped in the fastest product ramp in its history, with racks already running at major cloud providers including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

Nvidia returned about $28 billion to shareholders during the quarter. It has about $227 billion left under its buyback authorisation after the board added $150 billion in September.

The backdrop is unusual. Huang stepped down on 12 November. His resignation followed a board investigation, launched after he disclosed a relationship with a business executive accused of being a Chinese spy. The risk language in the release refers to the leadership transition, the search for a new chief executive and an ongoing review by an independent board committee. The stock had fallen about 24% in November before the report.

The question now is whether results this strong can separate the business from the boardroom. Demand for Nvidia’s chips looks firmly intact. Investors will focus on what Kress says about margins, the CEO search and the investigation, where any surprise could matter more than the quarter itself.  

ADDED:

Cash generation was just as strong. Free cash flow came to around $44 billion in the quarter, about double the level a year earlier. Nvidia also pointed to an agreement to acquire Hugging Face, the AI model platform, and said it had expanded Anthropic’s access to its Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers. Meta plans a wider rollout of Vera Rubin systems.

item.title: US stocks fall; Dow stocks are the hardest hit with a drop of 1.65%
item.description:
US stocks closed lower across the board, with the Dow Industrial Average leading the declines. Salesforce was a big drain, falling 9.41%, but the selling extended well beyond one stock. Twenty-five of the Dow’s 30 components finished lower.

Small caps also struggled, with the Russell 2000 losing 1.50%. The Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 held up better on a relative basis, but both still closed lower by roughly 0.7%. There was little comfort for buyers in the closing numbers.

During the session, reports of communications disruptions added uncertainty and coincided with flight-to-safety flows into Treasuries, gold, the CHF and JPY. Those were intraday moves; they did not prevent another lower close for stocks. images.investinglive.com

US closing levels

  • Dow Industrial Average: −849.06 points (−1.65%) to 50,764.09.
  • S&P 500: −76.06 points (−1.03%) to 7,340.53.
  • Nasdaq Composite: −181.37 points (−0.74%) to 24,328.38.
  • Russell 2000: −41.07 points (−1.50%) to 2,701.87.
  • Nasdaq 100: −195.37 points (−0.72%) to 27,001.78.

Salesforce leads the Dow percentage losers

Salesforce fell $20.21 to $194.62, closing near its session low of $193.41. Salesforce plunged 9.41% as software shares came under heavy selling pressure. A string of technology outages heightened concerns about software reliability and security, while competition from AI-native platforms remained an overhang. Salesforce has not been publicly linked to the reported disruptions. Technically, the price fell below both its 100 and 200 day MAs adding to the bearish bias.  

Other sizable Dow losses included:

  • Nike: −6.30% to $35.85.
  • UnitedHealth: −5.39% to $389.81.
  • IBM: −4.69% to $231.14.

  • Home Depot: −2.40% to $339.17.
  • Microsoft: −2.27% to $506.24.
  • Visa: −2.23% to $416.97.

The weakness reached across software, healthcare, financials and consumer shares. That breadth matters. Salesforce was a standout loser, but the Dow’s decline had plenty of participation.

Only five Dow stocks finish higher

The winners were few, and their gains were modest:

  • Cisco: +0.62% to $95.11.
  • Honeywell: +0.46% to $218.96.
  • McDonald’s: +0.39% to $275.73.
  • Caterpillar: +0.08% to $570.93.
  • Amazon: +0.05% to $257.89.

Among other large technology names, Apple slipped 0.25% and Nvidia fell 0.48%. Those declines were relatively contained compared with Salesforce and Microsoft, helping explain some of the Nasdaq’s relative resilience.

Other notable losers

Selling also hit software, travel, solar and consumer-related shares:

  • Intuit: −7.17%.
  • Strategy: −6.34%.
  • Alaska Air: −6.20%.
  • First Solar: −5.83%.
  • Chewy: −5.55%.
  • Deutsche Bank: −5.47%.
  • Whirlpool: −5.02%.

Nvidia’s earnings were the next scheduled test for technology sentiment, with the company due to report at 4:20 PM. investinglive.com

The trading lesson: Know how the index is weighted

Salesforce had the Dow’s largest percentage decline, but the Dow is price-weighted. Its point moves reflect dollar changes in component share prices.

UnitedHealth fell $22.21 per share, compared with Salesforce’s $20.21 decline. That gave UnitedHealth a larger negative Dow point contribution despite its smaller percentage loss.

For traders, the index is a useful barometer, but look underneath it. With 25 Dow stocks declining and the five winners posting only small gains, the closing weakness extended well beyond the headline loser.
